newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hog prices, output seen rising after report.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hog prices, output seen rising after report.

text.p: Hog prices are seen rising and production is expected to increase following a bullishly construed USDA quarterly Hogs and Pigs report, a Chicago Mercantile Exchange panel of livestock experts said Friday.

"Instead of a year when we originally looked at a pretty rough third and fourth quarter in 1997, we are going to have some pretty profitable hogs possibly all the way through the year," said panelist Jim Sigmon, vice president of Commodity Department for Securities Corporation of Iowa.
The U.S. Agriculture Department reported the total number of hogs on farms at 96 percent of last year's level, compared with an average forecast of 98.4 percent.
The breeding herd was put at 97 percent of a year ago versus an average estimate of 101.6 percent, and hogs kept for market at 97 percent of last year versus an average prediction of 97.5.

"The most bullish number, in my opinion, was probably the breeding herd figure at only 97 percent of last year when average analysts' estimates going into the report were almost two percent above a year ago levels," said panelist Dan Vaught, livestock analyst for A.G. Edwards.
Because of the low hog numbers, CME hog and pork belly futures are seen trading up their respective daily trading limits of 2.000 cents and 3.000 cents per lb on Monday.

Panelists agreed with CME traders that both futures contracts could rise the daily limit for more than one session before the market fully digests the report. Cash hog markets are also called higher due to the report and cash pork prices are seen firming, they said.
The report's "figures suggest far fewer pigs than pre-reports thought and therefore we should see quite a move up," said panelist Kelly Zering, extension specialist at North Carolina Stae University.
Panelists projected cash hog prices to range from $49 to $60 per cwt in the first quarter, $56 to $61 in the second quarter and $49 to $51 in the fall quarter.

But the higher prices and projected lower feed costs should spark stepped-up expansion of the herd, as seen in the report's December/February farrowing intentions which were put at 101 percent of a year ago.

"The farmers are thinking that they may want to increase their herds," especially with corn prices slipping, Sigmon said. "The last quarter could be where the surprise is to come as we see just exactly how enthusiastic these farmers are about expanding the herd."
The panelists also looked for live cattle futures and fed cattle prices to benefit initially from the bullish hog report.
Live cattle prices could gain another $1 per cwt next week and futures should also advance, especially if hog and pork belly futures are locked limit-up on Monday, they added.
